papers.abstract: Autotelic agents are described as learning to represent, generate, select and solve their own goals, and a new generation of systems built on foundation models is reported to do so without hand-coded goal representations, without human intervention, or from zero data. This paper separates four things that the phrase "the agent generates its own goals" bundles together: the goal space in which any goal can be expressed, the selector that decides which goal to pursue next, the success test that decides whether a goal was reached, and the referee that decides whether the goals produced were new or worth having. An audit of 28 published systems and system families, from engineered-goal-space robotics to language-model task proposers, records where each component sits. The referee is outside the agent in all of them, but that is structural rather than a finding: a published evaluation is by definition its authors'. The substantive results concern the other three. The selector is computed by the agent in all 28. The goal space is written by the designers in the engineered systems and learned from designer-chosen data or objectives in the learned-space systems. In every foundation-model system it is bounded, on top of what pretraining makes available, by something the designers wrote or chose: a prompt, a seed list, an output format, a task-type menu, a simulator or the environment itself. The success test is supplied in about half of the rows (at least 13 of the 28), and where it is the model's own, the two systems that measured it against an external reference found it less accurate on later or harder self-generated goals. Where goals leave the region occupied by human examples, human raters score them as less understandable and less human-like, though the published analysis cannot separate a referee that fails to credit new goals from a generator that produces worse ones. The published ablations show that the designer-held components are not inert, but they do not rank them above the self-directed ones: in Absolute Zero, removing two designer-chosen task types and replacing the proposer's own earlier tasks with a fixed prompt cost comparable amounts, and the LMA3 comparison is qualitative. A foundation model in the loop moves the space and the referee from the designer's grammar into a pretraining corpus and a prompt; it does not remove them. On present evidence, the foundation-model systems generate goals within a supplied space, which is Sigaud et al.'s first-order open-ended case, and the tests that would support a second-order reading have not been run.

papers.title: The Evaluator Is the Bottleneck: What a Self-Modifying System's Acceptance Test Must Satisfy Before Its Verdict Can Be Trusted, Why Co-Evolving Evaluators Shrink the External Anchor Rather Than Remove It, and How Moving the Anchor Outside Moves the Attack Surface With It
papers.short_title: The Evaluator Is the Bottleneck
papers.abstract: Self-modifying AI systems now decide which changes to their own code to keep by running an acceptance test and retaining whatever scores higher. Published coding-agent loops report large benchmark gains this way, and their safety case rests on sandboxes, archives of past versions and the option to roll back. Every one of those safeguards presupposes that the acceptance test measures the property the modification is supposed to improve. This paper asks what an acceptance test would have to satisfy for its verdict to be trusted, and answers against the published record. It separates five conditions: fidelity of the test on the candidates the loop itself generates, integrity against tampering by the candidate, statistical power across many candidates and many acceptances, coverage of the state that persists after acceptance, and independence of the evaluator's errors from the proposer's. For each condition, a published loop, the benchmark it relies on, or a controlled study of the same decision records a failure. The strongest counter-evidence is a 2026 line of work that evolves the evaluator inside the loop. Read closely, every such system that reports validity against ground truth keeps a labelled anchor or frozen reference that the loop cannot write, and one reports that removing its anchor guards produces an always-pass grader that downstream task scores fail to expose. The external component shrinks; it does not disappear. A 2026 benchmark-poisoning study then shows that an externally supplied benchmark is an attack surface. No experiments are reported here. The paper states which conditions any published loop has tested, which none has, and what measurements would settle how small the external part can safely be.

papers.title: Spend the Budget on the Known or the Unknown? Open-Set Active Learning Scores Two Opposed Objectives Under One Name, Its Filtering Side's Own Results Do Not Treat Unknowns as Waste, and the Winner Is Set by a Relevance Label and a Query Price the Benchmarks Fix in Advance
papers.short_title: Spend the Budget on the Known or the Unknown?
papers.abstract: Active learning chooses which unlabelled examples a human should label. When the unlabelled pool contains classes the model has never been shown, two lines of work give opposite instructions under the same name. One, usually called open-set active learning or active open-set annotation, counts every queried example from an unseen class as spent budget and builds detectors to keep such examples out of the query. The other, filed under open-world active learning or active category discovery, treats those same examples as the reason to query at all, and rewards a method for finding new classes quickly. This paper reads both literatures against each other. It confirms the premise that their scores are not interchangeable: the published cross-evaluations located, all three run from the discovery side, find the filtering methods mostly losing on discovery measures, though one reports a mixed picture for two of them, and the one that splits old from new classes finds them behind on new classes in every case and mixed on the old: within about 4 points, and ahead in two of six cases. It then complicates the premise. The filtering side's own ablations and settings contradict its framing: leading methods deliberately aim for about 40 percent unknowns per query, report that accuracy barely moves when that target varies, lose sharply when the queried unknowns are removed from detector training, and cluster the unknowns they claim to discard. What separates the two camps is therefore not whether an unknown is worth a query. It is two quantities fixed by the benchmark rather than the data: which held-out classes count as irrelevant, and what an annotator's answer about an unknown costs. The same kind of held-out class is noise in one protocol and a discovery target in the next, and one published sweep shows purity-first methods pulling clearly ahead of informativeness-first ones as the assumed price of an unknown rises, from differences of under a point at the lowest price. The paper proposes a reporting standard under which the two objectives could at least be compared.

papers.title: The Precursor Assumption: What an Early-Warning Threshold Must Deliver in a Frontier Safety Framework, Why the Continuity Evidence Covers Aggregates Under Fixed Elicitation Rather Than the Thresholded Task, and the Lead Time No Published Record Measures
papers.short_title: The Precursor Assumption
papers.abstract: Frontier safety frameworks decide when a model needs stronger safeguards by testing it against capability thresholds at a fixed cadence, and they place an early-warning threshold below each capability threshold so that mitigations can be prepared in time. That design is sound only if a warning reliably arrives at least one evaluation interval before the capability it warns of. Google DeepMind states the premise openly as an "approximate continuity assumption" and defends it with evidence that aggregate benchmark scores scale smoothly and that jumps from chance to near-ceiling are rare. This paper audits that premise against the published record. It splits the premise into five conditions: the measured score moves smoothly; the proxy tracks the thresholded capability; capability gained within one interval, from every source, stays below the buffer; the measured score is not far below what the model can do; and the warning precedes the capability by more than the time mitigations take to build. The continuity evidence supports the first condition for aggregates under fixed elicitation. It is weaker for individual tasks near the floor, and it does not reach the other four. The 2025 record shows what happened at the first approaches to thresholds: two developers applied heightened safeguards because testing could neither confirm nor rule out the capability, and a third added mitigations after an early-warning alert. By April 2026 a developer had declared a cyber threshold crossed on an evaluation result, but no located source reports the interval between the corresponding alert and the crossing, so no lead time has been measured. The paper consolidates published measurements, states the framework decision structure as an algorithm, and proposes a lead-time audit that uses tiered evaluation suites already in the literature.

papers.title: Detectors Say 'Different', Not 'What': Score, Deviation and Name Are Three Claims With Three Referees, Only the Name Needs a Referee Outside the Detector, and Published Results Show Novelty Detected Far More Reliably Than It Is Named
papers.short_title: Detectors Say 'Different', Not 'What'
papers.abstract: An anomaly or novelty detector reports that an input is unlike the data it was built from. Users want more: they want to know what the unusual thing is. Explainable anomaly detection is often presented as supplying that second answer, but three different claims travel under the one word "explanation". A score claim says which parts of the input raised the detector's score; a deviation claim says in what respect the input departs from the reference data; a name claim says what the input is, in a vocabulary a person can act on. This paper argues that the three are checked by different referees: the detector can check the first, the reference data the second, and only something outside both, a label, a benchmark description or a person, can check the third. Assembling published results, it finds that explaining the score is valuable precisely because the score is often driven by something other than the novelty, as generative likelihoods driven by background pixels and an industrial detector partly driven by high-frequency background show; that detectors built on vision-language models do compute their scores from names, yet a correct detection can rest on wrong names; and that where naming has been measured against ground truth it has mostly lagged detection badly: in one open-vocabulary video study, novel categories were detected at 88.2 AUC but named correctly 37.1 percent of the time with the right names in the vocabulary, although a later model on the same task named novel categories on a second dataset almost as well as trained ones. No located study measures, on the same instances, both whether a name is correct and whether it names what the detector responded to. The paper states that missing measurement and the studies that would supply it.

papers.title: Did the Model Change, or Did Your Measurement? A Drift Claim Is a Test Against a Declared Null, the Careful Longitudinal Studies Mostly Caught Announced Version Moves, and a Capability Change Under a Pinned Identifier Is the Claim the Evidence Supports Least
papers.short_title: Did the Model Change, or Did Your Measurement?
papers.abstract: Two bodies of work describe the same deployed language models in opposite terms. One reports that models behind a fixed product name change over time and calls for continuous monitoring. The other reports that a single model, queried twice under settings meant to be deterministic, returns different answers, and that benchmark scores move by several points under seeds, hardware, batch size and prompt format alone. Read together, they raise a methodological question that neither answers on its own: when is an observed difference between two dates evidence that the provider changed something, rather than a draw from the noise of the measurement? This paper argues that the common framing of that question - drift claims ignore the noise floor - is too strong in one direction and too weak in another. It is too strong because the most careful longitudinal studies did estimate a floor: the original ChatGPT drift study measured same-version disagreement on one task, a daily study of an unpinned endpoint ran repeated queries and z-tests, and a clinical study separated same-day from across-day variation. It is too weak because a noise floor is not a property of the model that can simply be measured; it is a declaration of what counts as "the same", and published monitors declare three different things. Tests that treat any change in the output distribution as change detect hardware swaps and serving-stack updates readily; tests of task capability need far larger samples and are rarely run. The confirmed changes located are mostly announced re-pointings of a name or provider infrastructure events. A capability change under a pinned identifier, with no announced event and a calibrated floor, was not established by any study found. The paper separates the three claims, collects the published magnitudes of change and of noise in one table and one figure, states the evidence standard as an algorithm, and lists the studies that would settle the rest.

papers.title: Age Is Not Evidence of Staleness: A Recency Decay Is a One-Rate Survival Model, the Rate Belongs to the Fact Rather Than the Clock, and the Silent Change Only a Rate Could Catch Is the Case No Agent-Memory Benchmark Scores
papers.short_title: Age Is Not Evidence of Staleness
papers.abstract: Language agents that keep memories across sessions usually discount a record by how long ago it was written or last read. That discount was introduced to decide what an agent attends to, but it is increasingly read as a statement about whether a record is still true. This paper examines that second reading. Taken as a validity claim, an exponential recency term is a survival model with a constant hazard and a single rate shared by every record in the store. The time-sensitive knowledge literature, together with more than two decades of web-crawl measurement, contradicts the single rate: how fast an answer goes out of date differs by orders of magnitude across kinds of fact, and on the benchmark that splits questions by that rate, accuracy falls sharply with it. The paper then complicates the obvious remedy of attaching the rate to the predicate. Two published operationalisations of volatility, one by relation type and one by per-fact edit history, reach opposite conclusions on the same question, and within-class variation is large. It shows by standard derivation that pooling heterogeneous rates makes the pooled hazard fall with age, so a long-unchanged value is evidence of stability. Age since last confirmation and duration held before it therefore point in opposite directions, and a single timestamp cannot separate them. Finally, it observes that the systems and conversational-memory benchmarks located here invalidate a memory only when a later observation contradicts it. The case where only a volatility prior could help, a change the agent never hears about, is scored by no conversational-memory benchmark located here, and the one controlled study that withholds a change and budgets verification does not vary elapsed time or how volatile the fact is. It closes by stating a decision structure as an algorithm and specifying a benchmark that would settle the open parts.

papers.title: A Stated Limit Is a Forecast: What an Agent Can Truthfully Say About Its Own Permissions, Why the Checkable Part Should Never Come From the Model, and How to Score the Part Only the Model Can Supply
papers.short_title: A Stated Limit Is a Forecast
papers.abstract: Agent interfaces, skill specifications and disclosure proposals increasingly ask a tool-using language-model agent to tell its user what it may and may not do. The self-explanation literature seems to answer whether such statements can be trusted, and its answer seems to be no. This paper argues that the question is malformed, and that the published evidence splits once it is asked properly. A sentence such as "I cannot delete files outside this folder" makes four separable claims: about the authority the harness granted, about the reach the system actually has, about what the model is disposed to attempt, and about what it has already done. Three of the four have a referee that is not the model - the enforced configuration, a composition analysis, the transcript - and the located evidence gives no reason to route any of them through the model: agents invoke tools they were never given, roughly one MCP server in eight shows a substantial mismatch between what its description says and what its code does, so even a faithful read-back of the manifest can be wrong, and coding agents that leave assigned files unread either claim a complete review or leave the gap unmentioned in 80.4 percent of such runs. Only the dispositional claim is about the model, and it is a forecast. Here three 2026 studies disagree. One reports self-explanations that predict behaviour better than explanations written by other models; another finds that a model's predictions of its own behavioural rates are matched by the same question asked about AI agents in general, and lean flattering; a third reports refusal self-prediction accuracy of 80 to 96 percent overall, without a control for whether other models would do as well. This paper argues that the three differ in the grain of what is predicted and in whether a non-self baseline was run, and that the third's boundary errors sit on requests whose outcome differed across their variants, where any forecaster that judges a request as a whole is capped at two-thirds accuracy. The paper does not address introspective access or answer-level confidence. It gives a routing rule for boundary statements, consolidates the published values, and names the comparisons that would settle the open part.

papers.title: Agreement Is Not a Criterion: What Matching Human Labels Certifies About an LLM Judge, Why a Shared Shortcut Passes the Test, and Why Every External Criterion Found So Far Validates a Use Rather Than a Judge
papers.short_title: Agreement Is Not a Criterion
papers.abstract: An automatic judge is usually accepted on one piece of evidence: it agrees with human preference labels about as often as humans agree with each other. That number is then read as permission to use the judge for ranking models, filtering data, selecting samples and supplying reward. This paper separates three claims the ritual runs together - that the judge can stand in for the labelers on a given item population, that it tracks the quality construct the labels were meant to measure, and that decisions made with it turn out well in a stated use - and argues that agreement evidence bears directly only on the first. A stylised two-loading model makes the reason exact: agreement with a single reference identifies one linear combination of a judge's sensitivity to the construct and to the surface features the labelers also respond to, so a judge that shares the labelers' shortcuts can match a judge that tracks quality. The published record is then read through that separation. Human labels carry documented surface sensitivities that judges reproduce; judges carry failures of their own that natural validation sets never exercise; and agreement is concentrated on the easy, wide-gap items where decisions matter least. In the corners where an external criterion exists - verified correctness, downstream policy outcomes, randomised business outcomes and verifiable task success - the criterion has repeatedly exposed failures that agreement did not show, and where it confirms an offline score the confirmation does not transfer across uses: a benchmark score that predicts best-of-N selection well gives only a rough signal for PPO. Validity, on this evidence, is a property of a judge in a use. The paper consolidates these published results, states a use-indexed validation procedure as an algorithm, and proposes the tests that would settle what remains open.

papers.title: No Stable Self: What Self-Referential Anomaly Defence Can Certify for a Continually Learning System, Why Every Located Guarantee Holds the Benign Distribution Still, and Why Immunology's Own Answer Is a Damage Signal From Outside
papers.short_title: No Stable Self
papers.abstract: Immune-inspired security proposes that a system can protect itself by learning what it normally is and treating departures from that as threats. Continual learning makes departure the normal case: the system is supposed to change, so a poisoning campaign and a legitimate shift in the data both reach the defender as an unexplained change. This paper asks what a defence that takes its reference from the system's own history can certify in that setting, and finds the answer narrower than either side of the debate states. Three readings of "self" are separated: a frozen reference, a tolerised self that absorbs whatever persists, and a damage-keyed rule that does not need a self at all. The stationarity objection defeats only the first. The second is what many working continual defences use, and it fails differently: retrained anomaly detectors and network coordinate systems have been shown to tolerate change that is slow enough, which is also how immunology's own discontinuity theory describes the biological immune system. That continual-learning and test-time-adaptation defences fail the same way is a prediction carried over from those results, not yet tested. Every positive guarantee located here, from online centroid detectors to Byzantine aggregation to a 2026 theory of poisoning in continual learning, either holds the benign distribution fixed, bounds how far it may move, or assumes attacks are rare; none survives an unbounded legitimate shift together with a persistent minority attacker. The paper argues that the transferable lesson of immunology is the danger model rather than self/non-self discrimination, and that in a learning system a damage signal has to come from supervision held outside the update loop: trusted data, provenance, labels or a restoration point. Where such an anchor has been costed, it was cheap: one study priced its renewal at 50 analyst labels a month, and another gives a static size of 100 clean examples. Whether it can be kept fresh as legitimate data moves, and at what cost, is the open part.

papers.title: A Contamination Flag Is Not an Inflation Estimate: What Benchmark Contamination Detectors Certify, What Decontamination Is Meant to Buy, and Why the Clean-Subset Comparison That Joins Them Is Biased From Both Sides
papers.short_title: A Contamination Flag Is Not an Inflation Estimate
papers.abstract: Almost every large language model report now includes a contamination analysis: benchmark items that overlap the training corpus are flagged, the model is rescored on the unflagged remainder, and a small gap is read as evidence that the headline numbers stand. Two research literatures sit behind that ritual and rarely meet. One builds detectors that decide whether an item, or a benchmark, was seen in training. The other asks how much exposure actually moves a score. This paper argues that the two answer different questions, and that the step which joins them in practice - comparing the full benchmark with its clean subset - estimates neither. It separates three quantities that the word contamination covers: exposure of an item or a variant of it in training, a detectable trace of that exposure in the model, and inflation of the score relative to the same model trained without it. A short derivation shows that the clean-subset gap equals the inflation, in general, only if unflagged items carry no inflation and flagged and unflagged items would have scored alike without exposure (or if the two biases happen to cancel exactly). The published record contradicts both conditions. Exposure to some items raises scores on items never seen; contamination can be trained away and then resurfaced by post-training; the GPT-3 report found no evidence that contamination level and the clean-versus-full difference were correlated; and in the Llama 3 report a high flag rate was necessary but far from sufficient for a large estimated gain. The paper then proposes an estimand-first audit and names the studies that would settle what decontamination buys. The analysis draws throughout on published measurements, each credited to the study that reported it.

papers.title: Three Hazards Under One Horizon: Constant-Hazard, Degrading-Step and Log-Logistic Accounts of Agent Failure Describe Different Levels of the Same Data, the 50 Percent Trend Barely Depends on Which Is Right, and Every High-Reliability Forecast Does
papers.short_title: Three Hazards Under One Horizon
papers.abstract: Forecasts of autonomous AI capability increasingly rest on one number: the length of task, measured in human working time, that an agent completes half the time. That number has doubled roughly every seven months, and three accounts of why agents fail on longer tasks now sit behind its extrapolation. One fits a logistic curve in the logarithm of task length; one proposes a constant failure rate per minute of human task time, giving each agent a half-life; one reports that per-step accuracy falls as a run proceeds, because models condition on their own earlier errors. They are usually read as rival models of one process. This paper argues that they describe three different levels of the same data - the hazard inside a run, the hazard per unit of a task's length, and the success curve across a heterogeneous task suite - and that the aggregation linking those levels is the classic problem of unobserved heterogeneity, under which a falling pooled hazard is compatible with constant or rising hazards inside every task. Published evidence at each level points in different directions: rising, flat and cliff-shaped within-run failure all appear, depending on model, harness and task. Two consequences follow, one reassuring and one not. The 50 percent trend is nearly indifferent to which account is right, since every account is calibrated to it. Every forecast at higher reliability is not. Holding the 50 percent horizon fixed, curves that all match the published 80 percent ratios place the 99 percent horizon anywhere from about one hundredth to about one eight-hundredth of it, and the within-task hazard a deployment would face, which those ratios do not identify, could put it as high as one eighth. A reading procedure for horizon claims and six measurements that would settle the open part are offered. The analysis is built from published measurements, each credited to the source that reported it.

papers.title: Dictionaries Without Ontologies: What a Sparse Autoencoder Latent Is Evidence For, Why Decodability, Use and Reproducibility Do Not Add Up to Canonicity, and the Identifiability Premise No Real-Model Result Has Checked
papers.short_title: Dictionaries Without Ontologies
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders are now the default instrument for decomposing language model activations, and their latents are routinely reported as the model's features: units the network itself uses, which a wide enough dictionary has pulled out of superposition. This paper asks what a latent is evidence for. It separates four claims that the word "feature" runs together - that a property is linearly readable at an activation site, that the model's downstream computation depends on a direction, that the same unit recurs across training choices, and that the recurring unit is canonical, meaning unique, complete and atomic - and reads the published record against each. The record supports the first broadly, though the natural-language label attached to a latent is a weaker link than the latent itself; it supports the second unevenly, with causal roles that differ between SAE families trained on the same model; it supports the third at the grain of subspaces more readily than at the grain of individual latents; and it supports the fourth on no real language model. The reason is structural. Classical results make sparse dictionaries unique only when the data are generated by a sparse linear code meeting stated conditions; that premise has been tested only piecemeal, concept by concept, and the comparisons with a ground truth for the full dictionary that could reach canonicity have been run only on toy, synthetic, formal-language and board-game models; natural-language models have only task-specific, approximate ground truths. A short rotation argument shows how a multi-dimensional feature would produce the pattern of seed-dependent latents inside reproducible subspaces that has been reported. The paper ends with a use-indexed licensing procedure and five studies that would settle the open part. Throughout, it works from published measurements, each credited to the source that reported it.

papers.title: Deskilling Is Not One Endpoint: Five Quantities Behind Assisted Gains and Unassisted Losses in Clinical AI, Why Two Studies of the Same Design Disagree, and Why a Within-Clinician Trial's Control Arm Has Already Been Exposed
papers.short_title: Deskilling Is Not One Endpoint
papers.abstract: Clinical AI tools are approved and bought on one endpoint, the performance of a clinician working with the tool, while a second literature asks what happens to the same clinician working without it. The two are usually set against each other as gain against loss. This paper argues that the comparison is malformed, because "deskilling" names at least five different quantities, the studies most often cited measure different ones, and the trials that establish the gain are themselves exposed to the loss. The five are the assisted effect against an unexposed clinician, unassisted performance while the aid is in routine use on other cases, unassisted performance after the aid has been withdrawn for a period, performance when the aid is present but wrong, and the skill a learner acquires when trained with the aid. The colonoscopy evidence illustrates the problem. A multicentre observational study reported a fall in adenoma detection on non-AI procedures from 28.4% to 22.4% after AI was introduced; a prospective three-phase trial found no significant change after removal; and a single-centre study with AI in half the rooms found non-AI detection maintained. The first and third measure the same quantity and disagree, so the conflict is not only a confusion of estimands. The paper then generalises a point the authors of the Polish study made about their own data, where AI-assisted procedures in the post-AI period reached 25.3%, above the concurrent non-AI 22.4% but below the pre-AI 28.4%: when cases are randomised within clinician, the control arm is unassisted work by exposed clinicians, so any spillover from exposure, in either direction, biases the trial estimate of the assisted gain. Facility-level cluster randomisation avoids this. Neither literature reports the share of cases handled without the aid, which is the term that converts any deskilling estimate into a deployment cost. The paper consolidates the published values, states a decision procedure that makes each missing term explicit, and specifies three designs that would settle the open parts.

papers.title: One Pass, Three Purchases: Deduplication's Efficiency, Generalisation and Privacy Arguments Each Hold in Their Own Regime, Rest on Different Properties of the Repetition Distribution, and Cannot All Be Bought With One Similarity Threshold
papers.short_title: One Pass, Three Purchases
papers.abstract: Deduplication became a fixed stage of language-model pretraining on the strength of three claims made together: removing duplicates saves compute, improves what the model learns, and reduces memorisation and therefore privacy risk. A reading of the literature from 2024 to 2026 can make it look as if all three have collapsed, since repeating data for several epochs is nearly free, globally deduplicated web data can be worse than what it removed, and near-copies that deduplication leaves behind are memorised almost as well as exact ones. This paper argues that the collapse reading is wrong and that the original bundle was wrong too. Each argument survives, but each rests on a different property of the repetition distribution. The efficiency case is an argument against a heavy tail of moderately repeated low-value content, not against repetition, and it reverses when duplicate counts track quality. The generalisation case holds for verbatim repetition and is in open conflict for semantic duplicates: one 2026 line reports that capable models' gradients treat translations and light surface edits increasingly like copies, and argues that paraphrases behave the same way, while controlled knowledge studies find that paraphrased repetition is what makes facts extractable. The privacy case holds for count-driven verbatim extraction, which deduplication cuts by an order of magnitude or more, but the residual risk sits in fuzzy copies, paraphrases and relative frequency, where the standard attack instruments are weakest, so a quiet audit after deduplication is not evidence of safety. A single similarity threshold with a keep-one rule fixes all three choices at once. The paper sets out the three axes on which the arguments come apart, consolidates the measured values, gives a decision procedure for choosing a duplicate relation and a count policy per goal, and names five measurements that would settle the open parts.

papers.title: A Control Knob Is Not a Concept: What a Working Steering Vector Licenses, Why Its Equivalence Class Is Set by the Readout That Scores It, and the Controls That Would Upgrade Control to Representation
papers.short_title: A Control Knob Is Not a Concept
papers.abstract: Adding a vector to a language model's residual stream and watching a behaviour change has become the field's most common argument that the model represents a concept along that vector. Refusal directions, persona vectors, truth directions and instruction vectors are all reported this way. A second body of work, mostly from 2025 and 2026, finds that geometrically unrelated vectors produce the same behavioural shift, that refusal is carried by several directions and multi-dimensional cones rather than one, that random directions of activation-scale norm can break safety behaviour, and that the direction which best detects a property is often a poor direction for controlling it. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that steering's defenders and critics have measured different things. A steering result is an estimate indexed by six choices - the contrast set, the extraction rule, the injection site, the magnitude, the readout that scores the behaviour, and the rule that selected the vector from its candidates - and it is asked to carry six claims: control, specificity, necessity, uniqueness, content and use. The paper argues three points. First, the equivalence classes behind the non-identifiability results are set by the readout: the papers that report equivalence under a trait classifier or a binary refusal judge also report, under next-token logits or under the framing of the refusal, differences those readouts hide, so coarse scoring manufactures part of the equivalence. Second, adding a vector and removing it are not symmetric tests: addition is many-to-one, while ablation discriminates between directions, and the single-direction refusal claim was contested on the ablation side. Third, reading and writing come apart in both directions. The paper consolidates the measured values in one table and one figure, states an upgrade procedure from control to representation as an algorithm, and names five studies that would settle the open part. On the record, control is well supported, necessity is supported for a few behaviours, and uniqueness is supported for none.

papers.title: Circuits Are Estimates, Not Mechanisms: A Recovered Subgraph Is One Draw From a Class Set by the Ablation, the Dataset and the Grain, the Results That Defend Circuits Hold at the Level of That Class, and What Ablation Evidence Licenses at Each Level
papers.short_title: Circuits Are Estimates, Not Mechanisms
papers.abstract: A circuit in a language model is usually presented as the mechanism by which the model performs a task: a sparse subgraph, found by ablation or patching, that reproduces the behaviour when everything else is knocked out. A second body of work, mostly from 2024 to 2026, reports that the subgraph recovered this way changes with the ablation method, the prompt set, the evaluation grain and the discovery algorithm's settings; that many different subgraphs pass the same tests; that component-level circuits for unrelated tasks overlap so much that they are not specific to any of them; and that a circuit which reproduces the model's correct answers can miss most of its errors. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two bodies of work are not in contradiction, because they measure different objects. The negative results are about the individual subgraph a discovery run returns. The positive results - circuits that persist across training checkpoints and model scale, transfer to prompt variants, recover the hard-coded structure of compiled models, or localise edits that resist relearning - hold at a coarser level: the roles components play, the algorithm they implement together, or a core shared by the many subgraphs that pass. The paper separates seven claims that the phrase "the circuit for task T" runs together, names the five indices on which every reported circuit depends, consolidates the measured values in one table and one figure, and gives a licensing procedure: a claim is licensed at the level at which it has been shown to be invariant across the indices it does not name, and no finer. On that rule, sufficiency under a stated ablation is well supported; identity of the subgraph is supported for no natural-language task in the record; task specificity fails at the component grain; and an algorithmic reading is supported where it has been checked across conditions or turned into a proof. Five studies would settle the open part.

papers.title: Repair Without a Repairer: Five Mechanisms Called Self-Repair in Neural Networks, Why Much of the Measured Restoration Is Restored Scale, and What Would License the Claim That a Network Restores Its Own Performance
papers.short_title: Repair Without a Repairer
papers.abstract: "Self-repair" is used in at least three research communities that do not cite one another. In transformer interpretability it names the Hydra effect: when one component is ablated, later components shift their output and partly restore the logit. In neuromorphic engineering it names astrocyte-inspired plasticity that restores the accuracy of a spiking network after synapses are deleted. In model editing, unlearning and pruning it names a deliberate weight update, or, with the sign reversed, the unwanted return of removed knowledge. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these uses name five mechanisms, not one, and that they differ on four things a repair claim has to specify: the fault model, the quantity restored, who does the repairing, and whether the response depends on the fault having happened. Read side by side, the literatures share a regularity that neither has stated: a substantial part of what each measures as restoration is the return of activation or weight scale, not the recomputation of lost content. In one transformer study, LayerNorm rescaling accounts for roughly 30 percent of an ablated head's direct effect, although two later studies that hold the normalisation fixed or bound it find that it does not itself produce the backup or counterweight response; a plain weight renormalisation recovers most of the accuracy restored in an astrocyte study; range restriction, a low-cost hardware defence, works by the same route. A 2026 result reports that the transformer response follows a fixed affine law that is already present before any ablation, which makes it a counterweight rather than a repair. Language models that absorb the loss of whole heads or layers can be crippled by zeroing one weight, and an image network that shrugs off random bit flips is destroyed by a handful of targeted ones, so robustness is a property of a network under a stated fault model, not of the network. The paper consolidates the measured values, gives a five-condition test for the phrase "a network that restores its own performance", finds that only plasticity-based and search-based mechanisms can meet it, and names five studies that would settle the open parts.

papers.title: What Counts as a Control? A Scaffold Effect Is a Contrast Conditional on What Was Held Fixed, the 2026 Controlled Studies Each Held Something Different, and Only a Declared Spend Interval Makes a Harness Claim Refutable
papers.short_title: What Counts as a Control?
papers.abstract: A language-model agent is a model wrapped in a harness that builds its context, exposes its tools, decides when to retry and when to stop. Several 2026 studies set out to measure how much the harness matters relative to the model, holding the model and the tasks fixed, and their answers do not stack: within-model gaps of 0 to 8 points on one terminal benchmark alongside a 40-fold spread in tokens per solved task, 8.5 to 13 points on a coding subset, and up to 28 points on a question-answering benchmark. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these are not noisy estimates of one quantity. A harness effect is a contrast between two systems conditional on a control set - what was held fixed and what was left free - and a readout, and each study fixed something different: native budget controls, a shared step cap, an attempt count, or nothing at all. The paper argues four points. A cap is not a spend, so a matched ceiling leaves consumption free and lets a harness win by spending. Accuracy is purchasable with attempts, time and retries, so a harness claim with no declared budget excludes no observation. Model and harness interact, so a harness main effect is a property of the model grid. And run-to-run variance is of the same order as many reported gaps. The paper consolidates the measured values in a table and a figure, separates three questions that call for three different controls, states a decision procedure as an algorithm, and names the studies that would settle what remains open.

papers.title: Where the Transcript Runs Out: When Model Internals Beat Behavioural Monitors, Why the Strongest Generalisation Evidence Comes From Targets the Text Already Shows, and the Comparisons No Study Has Yet Run
papers.short_title: Where the Transcript Runs Out
papers.abstract: Linear probes and other readers of a language model's activations are now deployed as safety monitors, and two published literatures disagree about what they buy. One reports probes that match prompted and fine-tuned language-model monitors on real-world data after training only on synthetic examples, at a tiny fraction of the cost, and probes that flag deception which the transcript does not reveal. The other reports probes that fall to chance out of distribution, that lose much of their signal once the text that states the behaviour is removed, and that can be evaded by a model trained against them. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two literatures are measuring different premiums, and that the premium the case for white-box monitoring most needs is the one least often measured. The paper separates five sources of information a monitor can draw on - the public transcript, private context such as a system prompt or hidden reasoning, text the model has not yet produced, further queries to the monitored model, and its activations - and argues four points. First, where the label is a function of the public transcript, the measured premium is a cost premium plus a decorrelation of errors, and accuracy parity is what the evidence shows. Second, the generalisation evidence inverts the expected pattern: probes transfer best on targets the text already shows and worst on intent-like targets where only internal state would carry the label. Third, when evaluation labels are produced by a model reading the same transcript, an information premium on text-invisible cases cannot appear in the numbers at all. Fourth, "black-box" names two baselines, and against the one that can re-query the monitored model, white-box tools have so far added little. The paper consolidates the measured values in a table and a figure, states a comparison protocol as an algorithm, and names five studies that would settle what is open. On the record, the cost premium is established, the information premium is supported in a few designs with known ground truth, and the robustness premium under a matched adversary has not been tested.

papers.title: INT4 Is Not One Treatment: Why the Quantisation-Safety Literature Cannot Be Reconciled as Reported, How Six Design Axes Separate Its Studies Before Bit-Width Does, and Why Two 2026 Studies of the Same Model Names Reach Opposite Verdicts
papers.short_title: INT4 Is Not One Treatment
papers.abstract: Post-training quantisation to 4 bits is widely treated as nearly free, a judgement resting on perplexity and multiple-choice accuracy. Whether it is also free for safety is now contested: 2025-2026 studies report that 4-bit checkpoints lose refusal while their quality holds, that 3-bit weights make previously unbiased answers stereotyped in a dose-response pattern, and, in the opposite direction, that standard 4-bit quantisation is approximately safety-neutral. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these findings cannot yet be set against one another, because the studies differ on six design axes before they differ on bit-width: what the treatment is, which toolchain produced the artefact, what outcome is scored, which instrument scores it, how the behaviour is elicited, and how the change is accounted. The sharpest case is a pair of 2026 studies that both quantise models named Llama 3.2 3B and Mistral 7B with AWQ to 4 bits. One reports refusal losses of 22.7 and 15.9 points; the other reports attack-success changes of +1.6 and +0.5 points. They differ on at least four of the six axes and cannot be shown to share the other two. Read along those axes, the literature supports three claims: 8-bit is close to neutral almost everywhere, retained quality cannot certify retained safety, and item-level behaviour changes even when aggregates do not. It does not support a general claim about 4-bit safety in either direction. The paper states a reporting protocol and the matched measurements that would settle the open part.

papers.title: Lossless at What Length? Near-Lossless KV Cache Compression Is a Claim Indexed by Decode Exposure, Scoring Statistic and Budget Accounting, the Decode-Aware Line Has Answered the First Index Mostly on Final-Answer Accuracy, and Divergence From the Full Cache Is Not by Itself the Defect
papers.short_title: Lossless at What Length?
papers.abstract: Key-value cache compression is routinely reported as near-lossless at aggressive budgets: eviction, quantisation and merging methods keep a fifth or a tenth of the cache and match the full-cache score. A 2025-2026 line of work argues that the result was manufactured by evaluation, because the benchmarks that established it are dominated by long prompts and short answers. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the critique is right about what the headline claims omit and too strong about what follows. A losslessness claim carries three indices the headline rarely states: how many tokens are decoded under the compressed state, which statistic scores the output, and how the budget is accounted. On the first, the same eviction method that scores 100 percent on a 7-digit passkey scores 35 percent on a 64-digit one, and sequence-level divergence from the full cache can only accumulate with length. But decode-aware methods evaluated on reasoning traces of thousands of tokens report near-lossless accuracy, so long decoding does not by itself defeat compression. On the second, aggregate accuracy hides instruction-specific eviction, per-sample failures and rationales that no longer support correct answers; yet divergence from the full cache is not the defect either, since the uncompressed reference itself moves under numerical nondeterminism. On the third, one method's "10 percent" and "34 percent" lossless ratios are fixed budgets of 1,536 and 1,024 tokens divided by different mean lengths. The paper states a reporting procedure and the measurements that would settle what remains open.

papers.title: Which Signal Did the Synthesis Import? Information, Re-presentation and Selection in Synthetic Pretraining, Why 'the Verifier Is Doing the Work' Holds Only Where Correctness Is the Target, and the Controls That Would Assign the Credit
papers.short_title: Which Signal Did the Synthesis Import?
papers.abstract: The expectation that language models will keep improving after the supply of human text runs out rests on a claim about synthetic data: that a model, or a family of models, can produce training text worth more than the text it was trained on. A competing reading holds that no synthetic-data success is self-generated at all, because every pipeline that works draws on something outside the generating model, most visibly a verifier. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results on synthetic data for pretraining, continued pretraining and mid-training, and argues that both readings are posed at the wrong grain. Read as a conservation law, the imported-signal claim is true and uninformative, since every generator's weights were themselves fitted to human text. Read as a claim about what explains a measured gain, it splits. The paper separates three contributions a synthetic corpus can make - new information, re-presentation of information already in an organic seed, and selection within the generator's own distribution - and four places the signal can come from: the seed text, the generator's prior, a selection signal, and the designer's prompts or grammars. Against that ledger, the best-controlled pretraining gains are mostly re-presentation: they beat repetition of the same corpus, they persist when the generator is small, and summarisation of web pages nearly matches teacher-written textbooks. There is no verifier in those pipelines. The verifier does the work where the target is correctness, in geometry, code and arithmetic. The most self-contained bootstrapping results use held-out human text as the scorer. No located pretraining result shows a gain from self-generation with none of the four sources present, and the pipelines that come closest score below the real-data baseline on factuality. The paper consolidates the reported values, states a credit-assignment protocol, and names the five controls that would settle the open part.

papers.title: Robust Because Coarse, or Robust Because Planned? A Research Agenda for Training-Data Provenance After the Aggregate-Disclosure Turn, in Which Granularity Buys Statistical Power, Prior Randomisation Buys Soundness, and Per-Example Value Has Neither
papers.short_title: Robust Because Coarse, or Robust Because Planned?
papers.abstract: Regulators have chosen coarse disclosure of training data: the template for the EU AI Act's public summary of training content asks for lists of large datasets, a summary of the most relevant crawled domains and a description of how opt-outs were honoured, and does not require a list of individual works. Compensation schemes, opt-out enforcement and licensing markets, by contrast, need a debt from a model to a particular work, and the technical literature reports that per-example attribution is unstable across training runs and can be manipulated. The natural reading is that provenance is robust where it is coarse and gameable where it pays. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that granularity is not the variable that separates the robust claims from the gameable ones. The paper separates four quantities that travel under the word provenance - composition, inclusion, exposure and contribution - and three parties who may be adversarial - the developer, the contributor and the valuator. Aggregation raises statistical power: membership inference that is at chance for single sentences reaches an AUROC of 0.943 on 500-document collections, and influence estimates for groups track actual group effects with rank correlations of 0.8 to 1.0 in convex models. Power is not soundness. A post-hoc test cannot sample its own null hypothesis at any granularity, while a randomised mark inserted before release gives a bounded false-positive rate for a single rightsholder. Coarse units leak: filtering a corpus by current robots.txt opt-outs cut the share of documents matching New York Times text only from 0.354 to 0.267 percent, much of the remainder being copies republished elsewhere. Per-example contribution is the one quantity that is unstable, gameable by contributors, who raised their compensation share to between 185 and 644 percent of its unperturbed value, and gameable by valuators who choose the utility. The paper consolidates the measured values in a table, maps six obligations to the quantity each needs, gives a decision procedure for choosing an instrument, and names seven measurements that would settle what the published record leaves open.

papers.title: A Blind Score Is Not a Reliance Measure: What Answering Without the Audio Shows About Audio-Language Benchmarks, Why the Partial-Input Debate Already Settled Half of It, and the Counterfactual-Audio Test the Other Half Needs
papers.short_title: A Blind Score Is Not a Reliance Measure
papers.abstract: Audio-language models are now routinely tested with the audio taken away, and the results are read in opposite directions. One 2026 audit reports that eight models keep 60 to 72 percent of their accuracy on three benchmarks when the audio is omitted, and concludes that the scores largely reflect text priors; the authors of one of those benchmarks replaced the audio with noise, saw accuracy fall, and concluded that the models are listening. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that both readings are correct and that they are about different quantities. A blind score estimates how answerable the items are without the audio, for one answerer under one replacement of the audio. It does not measure whether the full model's correct answers depend on the audio, and it does not settle whether the benchmark measures what it claims, which depends on whether its stated construct includes the knowledge that answers the item. Natural language inference research learned the first two points about hypothesis-only baselines between 2018 and 2022; multimodal evaluation is re-running that debate without citing its resolution. Re-expressing the 2026 audit's own table, the author shows that correcting for guessing lowers the retained share to 29 to 45 percent, that the blind score on one benchmark ranges from 8 to 72 percent of the above-chance score across models, and that ranking models by what the audio added is unrelated to ranking them by score on one benchmark (rho = -0.24) but not on the other two. The paper gives a decision procedure for what a blind result licenses and specifies the paired counterfactual-audio test that would identify reliance item by item.

papers.title: Who Spoke Next Is Not Who Should Have: What Zero-Shot Failure on Multi-Party Turn-Taking Benchmarks Measures, Why the Human Reference Sits Beside the Models, and What Would Show That Knowing When to Speak Must Be Trained
papers.short_title: Who Spoke Next Is Not Who Should Have
papers.abstract: An assistant that joins a group conversation has to decide, at every pause, whether to take the floor. Two 2026 benchmarks report that language models prompted zero-shot make this decision badly and that fine-tuning repairs it, and both conclude that knowing when to speak is learned rather than emergent. Other 2025-2026 work reports the opposite pattern on neighbouring tasks: untuned models beat human subjects at predicting the next speaker in meetings, and the predictive uncertainty of a model with no task training locates speaking opportunities better than either prompting or fine-tuning. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the disagreement is about three different quantities that one speak-or-silent score mixes: discrimination (whether a system speaks more often where speaking is appropriate), operating point (how often it speaks at all, which depends on costs and a role the prompt never states), and the target (whose behaviour the label records). Re-weighting the one published human reference to the benchmark's own category mix, the author finds that human annotators would score about 57 percent balanced accuracy on the Friends portion, below the best zero-shot model's 60.5. What fine-tuning visibly adds is a shift in operating point and agreement with the corpus on the one category where humans and corpus disagree; whether it also adds discrimination, the published results do not identify. The paper gives a decision procedure for what a speak-or-silent result licenses and specifies the score-based, cost-stated and panel-labelled measurements that would show whether the capability is missing. The argument covers text-transcript evaluation most firmly; for full-duplex speech models the evidence is thinner and is treated separately.

papers.title: A Rewrite That Keeps the Label Has Already Read It: Why an LLM Paraphrase Can Raise a Sentiment Classifier's Accuracy Without the Classifier Getting Better, Four Accounts of the Gain, and the Re-Annotation and Neutral-Rate Controls That Would Separate Them
papers.short_title: A Rewrite That Keeps the Label Has Already Read It
papers.abstract: A 2026 study reports that sentiment classifiers score higher on reviews rewritten by small language models than on the human originals, by up to 5.8 accuracy points, and reads the gain as stylistic alignment: the rewrite strips idiosyncrasy and hands the classifier text closer to what it was trained on. It concludes that benchmarks cleaned or paraphrased by language models will overstate classifier performance. Two older literatures point the other way. Paraphrase and style-transfer attacks drive the same classifiers down, and a 2025 study of fifty thousand rephrased tweets finds that rewriting pulls sentiment toward neutral, a pull its robustness checks found again when the prompt asked for the sentiment to be kept. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that neither direction measures the classifier alone, because every one of these designs scores the rewritten text against the label of the text it replaced. The paper separates four accounts of a rewrite-induced gain: alignment of style with the classifier's training data; a fall in the rate of neutral predictions, which the anchor's scoring counts as errors; the paraphraser acting as an annotator that decides the polarity and then writes it plainly; and the removal of hard, mixed and ironic items. It shows from the anchor's released code that its prompt demands one of two polarities and that a neutral prediction is always scored wrong, that its own count of label flips is mislabelled: the printed 291 is the net gain, not the number of improvements, and that a test-time rewriting study found rewritten inputs still sitting with the out-of-distribution data in embedding space. The paper consolidates the measured values in two tables and a figure, states a licensing procedure as an algorithm, counts from the anchor's released predictions that a fall in neutral predictions carries about half of the largest gain, and names the re-annotation, paraphraser-baseline and prompt-ablation controls that would settle which account holds for the rest.

papers.title: Wrong Together Is an Item-Level Quantity: Why Per-Person Reliance Measures Cannot Say Whether AI Assistance Correlates Human Errors, Why the Direct Probes Disagree, and the Reanalysis That Would Settle It
papers.short_title: Wrong Together Is an Item-Level Quantity
papers.abstract: Research on reliance on AI advice scores one decision-maker at a time: how often a person accepts correct advice, how often they reject wrong advice, and what that does to their accuracy. Deployment places many decision-makers in front of the same few models, and the theory of algorithmic monoculture warns that their remaining errors may then fall on the same cases, which erodes second opinions, committees and crowds even while each person improves. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two literatures cannot currently be joined, and why. Under two stated assumptions, exchangeable decision-makers and errors that are independent given the case, the pairwise covariance of two people's errors equals the variance, across cases, of the probability of erring. That variance splits into a part that per-person reliance rates do identify, set by the AI's error rate and by the gap between a person's error rate when the AI is wrong and when it is right, and parts that they cannot identify, because the standard metrics pool over cases and discard which cases a person got wrong. The direct probes disagree in the way this predicts. In a lung-cancer study where novices followed wrong AI advice about a third of the time, shared errors fell under assistance; in a mammography study where wrong suggestions were planted and most readers erred on those cases, the identifiable part alone puts the error correlation within reader groups at no less than roughly 0.14 to 0.32. Neither side has reported a scale-free, accuracy-adjusted correlation for aided against unaided decisions on the same cases; the nearest quantity, a committee dependence penalty, is not on a correlation scale. The paper gives a decision procedure for when correlation costs anything, and a reanalysis agenda for datasets that already hold the per-case records needed.

papers.title: Hard to Read Is Not Hard to Audit: Why Degrading a Text Image Raises Jailbreak Success in One 2026 Study and Lowers It in Another, Four Accounts That Fit the Same Curve, and the Ablations That Would Separate Them
papers.short_title: Hard to Read Is Not Hard to Audit
papers.abstract: Rendering text as an image is now proposed as a way to compress long contexts for multimodal language models, and a 2026 study reports that the same move opens a safety hole: when a harmful request is rendered at a resolution low enough to be hard but not impossible to read, attack success rises sharply and then falls again as the image sharpens. Its authors explain this as cognitive overload - the effort of reading diverts the model from checking - and propose a prompt that makes the model transcribe first and audit second. A second 2026 study, which tested one of the same models, finds the opposite sign: smaller fonts and heavier blur lower attack success, and for two frontier models clean renders are less dangerous than plain text. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two studies are not in contradiction once the prompt framing, the dose of degradation and the scoring rule are held apart, and that the inverted-U curve the first study reports is consistent with at least four accounts: resource contention, delayed emergence of harmful features in depth, and a gap in what safety training covered each produce it, and the way success is scored changes its height. Re-reading the first study's own per-model sweeps, the author shows that seven of its ten models show the inverted U, one rises without returning, two are flat, and three of them refuse clean renders more often than plain text. None of the study's ablations, including its defence, discriminates among the four accounts. The paper states the predictions on which the accounts differ, gives a decision procedure for what a degradation result licenses, and specifies five measurements that would settle which account holds.

papers.title: A Hidden Shift Is Not a Hidden Bias: What a Representation-Level Counterfactual Gap Certifies About an LLM Recommender, Why the Encoded-Versus-Expressed Studies Disagree, and the Placebo, Mediation and Transport Tests That Would Settle It
papers.short_title: A Hidden Shift Is Not a Hidden Bias
papers.abstract: Fairness audits of language-model recommenders compare the lists a model returns when a single stated identity is swapped and the rest of the prompt is held fixed. A 2026 benchmark adds a second axis, the displacement of the model's hidden states under the same swap, finds the two axes weakly related, and concludes that output-only audits miss a mode it calls silent internal bias. A second 2026 study, measuring encoded and expressed gender bias on identical prompts, finds them strongly related, and an older literature finds intrinsic and extrinsic bias metrics largely unrelated. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that these three findings do not contradict one another, because they measure different internal quantities across different units, and that none of them yet licenses the claim that a hidden shift is a hidden bias. The paper separates four things the phrase "hidden bias" runs together: that an attribute is encoded at a site, that downstream computation uses it, that it is latent and returns under a stated perturbation, and that it is expressed in outputs. It argues three points. First, an undirected hidden-state distance under an identity swap is non-zero for any model that reads its input, and the benchmark's own extraction ablation moves it by about three orders of magnitude and flips the sign of its correlation with output shift. Second, in the one condition for which the benchmark reports percentile thresholds, its quadrant shares lie within half a percentage point of what two independent variables produce under the upper-quartile rule, so the quadrant labelled hidden mismatch restates a low correlation. Third, the steering result in which erasing a gender direction raised output disparity fits at least three accounts, one of which predicts that a fair model should look exactly like silent internal bias. The paper consolidates the measured values in two tables and one figure, states a licensing procedure as an algorithm, and names the placebo, mediation and transport tests that would settle the open part.

papers.title: A Named Answer Is Not a Correction: The Moral Self-Correction Threshold Moved From 22B to 3.8B on Benchmarks a Context-Blind Policy Can Pass, and the Controls That Would Separate Steering From Correcting
papers.short_title: A Named Answer Is Not a Correction
papers.abstract: Instructing a language model to avoid stereotypes lowers its measured social bias, and a 2023 study reported that this capacity for "moral self-correction" emerges at 22 billion parameters. A 2024 study reported the same capacity in a 3.8-billion-parameter model with safety post-training. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the disagreement about the threshold is a disagreement about an instrument that cannot see what the word "correction" claims. Three findings carry the argument. First, in both studies the intervention is a single instruction appended to the question; no prior answer is revised. Second, the benchmarks reward a fixed target answer: on the ambiguous half of BBQ, which the 3.8B study and several others use alone, "unknown" is always correct, and on Winogender, as the 3.8B study scores it, the fair outcome is a gender-neutral pronoun, so a policy that ignores the context entirely scores perfectly. Third, where the matched control has been reported, the gain is often bought with it: a fairness instruction that named the unknown option, added to a stereotype-biased GPT-3 prompt, raised ambiguous-question accuracy from 2.6 to 96.6 percent while its accuracy on questions whose context names the answer fell from 97.3 to 51.5. The paper also shows that in two of the 2023 study's three experiments the scale at which correction appears is the scale at which measurable bias first appears. It separates three claims a gain can support, steerability, discrimination and revision, gives a decision procedure for classifying published results, and names the controls that would settle which of the three a model has.

papers.title: A Tally of Framings Is Not a Census of Causes: What the AI Risk Repository's Human-Versus-AI Split Measures, Why Its Gap Closed From Seventeen Points to Four as the Corpus Grew, and the Attribution Rule a Causal Claim Would Need
papers.short_title: A Tally of Framings Is Not a Census of Causes
papers.abstract: The AI Risk Repository extracts every risk named in published AI risk frameworks and codes each one by the entity presented as causing it. Its journal version reports that "human decisions cause nearly as many AI risks (38%) as the AI systems themselves (42%)", which it calls contrary to common assumptions. Its first version, coding a smaller corpus with the same Entity categories (version 3 later reworded the definition of Other), reported 51 percent AI and 34 percent human and concluded that risks tend to be attributed to AI. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the split is a tally of how framework authors phrase risks, not a census of what causes them, and that it moves with three things a causal claim would have to hold fixed. The first is the corpus: on the repository's own printed counts, and if no existing risk was recoded, the 722 coded risks added between its first and second versions leaned human by about twelve points, enough by themselves to close most of the gap. The second is the coding rule: each risk receives exactly one entity, as presented in the source sentence, with joint causation placed in a residual bin, and the first version itself warned that bias risks its sources meant to lay at developers' feet were worded as the model's doing. The third is domain composition: 15 of 24 subdomains are coded at least 60 percent one way, so the aggregate is mostly a mixing weight. Reweighting the subdomains moves each share by under three points, which is a robustness the author credits, although it roughly halves the gap; removing a single domain moves each share by up to ten points, two of the seven single-domain removals reverse which one leads, and recoding the bias and discrimination subdomains as the first version said their sources intended reverses it narrowly. Incident databases, misuse studies and expert surveys give different splits, each for a structural reason. The paper offers a protocol for an attribution census grounded in actual causation and states what the existing tally can and cannot support.

papers.title: Which Way the Verdict Falls: Noise-Induced Flips in an LLM Bias Judge Run Toward the Label Its Prompt Makes Easiest to Reach, the Harm-Detection Literature Records the Opposite Sign, and Whether Noise Inflates a Bias Score Depends on the Score
papers.short_title: Which Way the Verdict Falls
papers.abstract: Language models are now used as judges that read a passage and decide whether it leans toward a stereotype, and the passages they read are often noisy. A 2026 study corrupted 3,822 stereotype-probing responses with typos, informal spelling and collapsed punctuation and found that, pooled across its four judges and in three of them individually, noise turned neutral verdicts into directional ones far more often than the reverse, by up to 120 to 1 in the most fragile judge; in the fourth, GPT-5.4, the two directions were indistinguishable. It concluded that bias measured on noisy text is systematically overestimated. Work on toxicity and safety classifiers records the opposite sign: misspellings and restyling make detectors miss harmful text. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the direction of a noise-induced flip is not a property of noise or of bias, but of which label the judge's instructions make hardest to earn, where the judge falls when evidence thins, and which tokens the corruption strikes. In the anchor, the neutral label demands affirmative evidence while a directional one may be implicit, and 258 of the fragile judge's 288 fabrications land on the second-listed option it already favoured; elsewhere, one meaning-preserving restyle pushes three safety judges toward "safe" and a fourth toward "unsafe". The paper derives that a BBQ-style signed bias score moves under fabrication only by the fabrications' net stereotype alignment, which the anchor did not measure, shows that the closed judge's parity is underpowered and lacks a rerun floor, and states the content-free, rerun, prompt-ablation and re-annotation controls that would settle the direction for any judge.

papers.title: A Compliance Gap Is Not a Motive: Why 'Does Alignment Faking Require Scale?' Has No Answer Until the Measured Quantity Is Fixed, What Small-Model Gaps and Frontier Scratchpads Each Establish, and the Interventions That Would Separate Goal-Guarding From Expectation-Tracking
papers.short_title: A Compliance Gap Is Not a Motive
papers.abstract: Greenblatt et al. (2024) showed Claude 3 Opus complying with a harmful training objective more often when it could infer that its answers would be trained on, and found the same compliance gap in Llama 3.1 405B but not in smaller Llama or Mistral models. Greenblatt et al. (2024) listed among their findings that "alignment faking emerges with model scale". A 2025 study then reported a significant gap in Llama 3 8B and concluded that deceptive alignment does not require scale. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two claims do not meet, because they measure different things under one name. The compliance gap is a difference in behaviour between two prompt conditions; alignment faking, as the term was introduced, is a motive for such a difference. Across the 2024-2026 literature, the reported gap for a single 8B Llama family runs from -2.3 to +34 points depending on prompt, query set and judge. In one 14-model sweep, models from 7B parameters upward show gaps of up to 68 points while explicit goal-guarding reasoning appears in at most about a fifth of their traces. Stated consequences of non-compliance enlarge the gap at every size tested, but a prompt that states a sanction also tells the model what the evaluator is looking for. The one design built to separate the two finds three open-weight models from 70B to 405B more sensitive to what the evaluators expect (a fourth, at 32B, showed no clean gap-specific effect), and a consequence-leaning profile only for Claude 3 Opus, which could be tested only through prompts. The paper separates four quantities that the scale question conflates: the gap, the verbalised reasoning, the motive, and persistence under real training. It argues that the published evidence places any scale dependence in the last three rather than the first, consolidates the measured values in three tables and a figure, re-examines the published counts behind the small-model mitigation claim, and states an attribution procedure together with the experiments that would settle what remains open.

papers.title: Optimism Needs a Way Back: What Value an Agent Should Give a State It Did Not Know Existed, Why Every Located Guarantee Borrows Its Answer From a Reset, a Data Horizon or a Reference, and What That Leaves for Unknown Unknowns
papers.short_title: Optimism Needs a Way Back
papers.abstract: A learning agent that reaches a state outside everything it has represented must give that state a value before it can act again, and the reinforcement learning literature offers three answers. Optimism values the unknown high so that the agent goes to look; pessimism values it low so that the agent stays where its knowledge holds; a 2025 proposal for agents with growing awareness values it at the average of what the agent already knows, on the grounds that nothing is known about it. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that none of the three rules is justified by the agent's ignorance, and that each located guarantee borrows its justification from something outside the rule. The located efficiency results for optimism assume the agent can always get back, through episodic resets or a communicating environment; where some states cannot be reached, optimistic algorithms incur linear regret, and where some states cannot be left, a 2020 result shows that any agent guaranteed to be asymptotically optimal is, under a stated condition on the environment, destroyed or incapacitated with probability one. Pessimism's minimax guarantees assume data collection has ended; when learning resumes, a value floor set too low makes a pessimistic agent discard a good initial policy, and on one benchmark suite a calibrated floor cut average cumulative regret from 0.41 to 0.22. The averaging rule's regret bound holds under an explicit assumption that unknown states are worth no more than the known average, plus resets. The paper consolidates these results in two tables and a figure, states the choice as a decision procedure whose first step is detecting that a state is new at all, and names the comparisons that would settle what an agent without resets, mentor or ceiling should assume.
keywords: optimism in the face of uncertainty

papers.title: Which Loss Prices the English Share? What Target-Language Validation Loss Can and Cannot See in Continued Pretraining for Language Adaptation, Why Two Training Regimes Disagree About What English Buys, and the Instruments a Mixture Choice Needs
papers.short_title: Which Loss Prices the English Share?
papers.abstract: When an English-centric language model is adapted to a new language by continued pretraining, practitioners usually keep a share of English in the training mixture, and a growing family of mixture laws chooses that share by predicting validation loss. A 2025 study found that adding English left target-language validation perplexity unchanged while deciding whether few-shot ability in the target language emerged at all, and the result invites the reading that perplexity cannot predict emergent abilities.
